content: The Consolidated Strategic Information Guidelines for Viral Hepatitis: Planning and Tracking Progress Towards Elimination, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in February 2019, provides a comprehensive framework for collecting, analyzing, and utilizing data to combat viral hepatitis. This document is designed to assist national program managers in developing strategies to eliminate hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. It emphasizes the importance of strategic information in guiding policy and program decisions at local, national, and international levels. The guidelines outline the WHO's approach to monitoring and evaluating hepatitis B (HBV) and hepatitis C (HCV) programs. This includes surveillance of acute and chronic infections, as well as the sequelae of these infections, such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Surveillance activities are critical for understanding the epidemiological trends of hepatitis, identifying new infections, and assessing the impact of prevention, testing, and treatment interventions. The WHO's monitoring and evaluation framework follows a results-based approach, focusing on inputs, outputs, outcomes, and impacts. The framework also highlights the need for robust data systems to support these efforts, without creating unnecessary new systems. The document emphasizes the importance of five core interventions to achieve hepatitis elimination: (1) hepatitis B vaccination for infants, (2) prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HBV, (3) ensuring blood and injection safety, (4) harm reduction services for people who inject drugs, and (5) widespread testing and treatment. Specific targets for 2030 include 90% coverage of hepatitis B vaccination, 90% prevention of mother-to-child transmission, 100% blood and injection safety, and 90% diagnosis and 80% treatment of eligible patients. The guidelines also provide detailed recommendations for surveillance activities, including syndromic surveillance, enhanced case reporting, and biomarker surveys. Syndromic surveillance captures trends in acute hepatitis cases, while enhanced case reporting uses clinical and biomarker criteria to identify confirmed cases. Biomarker surveys are the gold standard for estimating the prevalence of chronic infections and guiding testing and treatment strategies. This can be achieved through data abstraction from clinical records, cancer registries, and vital registration systems. The WHO's Global Reporting System for Hepatitis provides a mechanism for countries to report these data. The document also addresses the integration of hepatitis surveillance with other health-related surveys, such as those for HIV, tuberculosis, and chronic diseases. Ethical considerations, such as informed consent and linking individuals to care, are emphasized when using stored specimens for additional testing. Overall, the guidelines serve as a high-level resource for national program managers, providing practical tools and protocols to strengthen hepatitis surveillance, monitor progress, and achieve the global goal of eliminating viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030.
